utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: "Resubordination of the TO units in the territory of the area of responsibility of the 9th Corps shall be conducted only upon my special order or approval." Shall I read on?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Now read 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: "Commanders of regiments or brigades may resubordinate and relocate units within their composition upon my approval." Let me explain a principle that is in use here. Whatever is subordinated to you may not be resubordinated by you to somebody else. Here, in this document, we see that the corps commander subordinated some units to the command of a regiment or a brigade and then commander of that regiment or a brigade can resubordinate that units to another regiment or brigade. The commander here is hereby banning any such action in the future, saying that it may not be done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we need English translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the principle of resubordination of the TO units. The JNA units were the only ones who were authorised to carry out combat operations in a certain zone and all units which were in that zone were subordinated to the commander. It is possible that certain operations in a certain area may be carried out by the Ministry of the Interior and that, if -- and that if -- however, if there were any JNA units there or TO units, then all of them had to be subordinated to the commander of the largest unit. So no matter whose unit it was, if it was the largest, then all other units had to be subordinated to the commander of the largest unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before we adjourn I would like to show the document, one more document. I'm sorry, it's 65 ter number 2057. This document is dated 19 November 1991 and it says "Disposition of Forces."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you could read the initial part? Starting in connection with your document.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Let me first say something. There are many such documents, similar to this one, which failed to mention the addressee. We don't know who this document was sent to. It says at the top, "Command of the 2nd tactical group" and so on, and then this document has to do with the disposition of forces. It says, "Forwarded" but it doesn't say forwarded to whom. "Pursuant to your document," such and such, "dated 19th of November 1991, we hereby send the disposition of forces to you." What we should ask ourselves is who is this document intended for and who was it sent to? Then we can draw conclusions on who was in charge for that area of responsibility. It says here the TO detachment M --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you could read the part with the first slash, dash, just, no can you please scroll up? Yes. It starts with, first Z-O-D-T-O-M. So the whole part.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: That means the first joint detachment of Territorial Defence M. It's known as M, the detachment. It is to control the roads which go from Bosnia-Herzegovina over through the Korana river to Slunj, with the following disposition. The first platoon goes there and so on. I don't know anything about this. This document is not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: What I heard -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have one specific question about this document. And it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This is in relation to assignment of TO units to military operation, their assignment to the respective military units. What would be the right procedure if a command of a military unit wanted to use a TO unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The unit would ask the commander to resubordinate the given TO unit and once it is resubordinated to that particular person, he will then issue orders and tasks to the TO unit, because all TO units can be resubordinated to a different commander, but not the command itself. All of its units can be resubordinated. If you look at what it says here, the 1st joint TO detachment and all the other units, they have all been resubordinated but not the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, you said the unit would ask the commander. Which commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Of these units. I don't know who this document was intended for. It says delivered but delivered to whom? Which area of responsibility is this? And why is this being delivered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic -- Mr. Maksic, you meant the unit would ask the respective TO commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He cannot order resubordination. He can merely ask for approval that these units be resubordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to this document being tendered into evidence. The witness stated that he didn't know anything about the document, that he wasn't familiar with the document, that he didn't know who it was sent to or why. He cannot grasp the significance of the document. We submit that the document should not be admitted into evidence on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The purpose to submit this document was to show the subordination of TO units to the army units, in this case it was command of the 2nd Tactical Group which is part of 9th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, the objection is that because the witness is not able to cast any light on the document, it should not be admitted. What's your response to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The witness doesn't know anything about this document. I agree with this. However, he knows the way how the TO units are assigned to the military units. So this is just an example of one of the assignments of TO units to the military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but you are telling us that it is one of the examples. The witness has not said it is one of the examples. The witness says he doesn't know anything about it. If the witness has to tell us how units are subordinated, can't he do so without using this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He can do. I don't have any objection not to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Then can we mark the document for identification and then we'll deal with it later. We are five minutes into our time. Shall we adjourn? We will come back at half past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Richterova, if that document that you were dealing with can be given an MFI number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number or MFI number 131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, just for the sake of clarification, many times during your testimony you mentioned these TO units existed only on paper. Which units, which TO units, did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the units of the TO Staff of Banija, Lika and Kordun. I meant those of the TO staffs in Krajina. There were municipal units; however, the Krajina TO staff as such did not have a single unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify this point. Before the adjournment, we talked about various units which were subordinated to the 9th Corps of the JNA. Which unit could participate during this -- these operations above those military units? You mentioned TO. Were there some other units which could participate in these operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: There were JNA and TO units, including the units of the Ministry of the Interior, if any, and where necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When such an operation was in the preparation stage, were there any meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: All the prospective participants in an operation would first meet to present their own possibilities and thus conduct coordination, and then they would agree on the time and the area where the operation would be carried out and then the person in charge of the operation would plan combat activities and work on the combat documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If police units were involved in such an operation, who would be present during a meeting on behalf of these units?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: First of all the units of the Ministry of the Interior were not able to be resubordinated to the JNA units without prior approval of the Minister of the Interior. Such meetings were attended by an organ of the Ministry of the Interior. Where the operation at hand was of higher significance, the Minister of the Interior may have attended the meeting as well or his representatives in charge thereof. In the ministry, they also had a person in charge of operative matters, planning, and so on. Therefore, the Minister of the Interior could appoint his representative, who would have a certain remit of powers, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would Minister of Interior of aware of the main goal or main task of an operation? And I will be more specific. In case that a police unit participates in this operation, would the Minister of Interior be informed about the main goal of this operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: When an operation was thoroughly planned out, commands or orders would be written detailing duties of all the participants. Such documentation would also be delivered to the Minister of the Interior, in so far as he had to be informed of the participation of his units. He may have been sent an entire order or only a part of it. For instance, the commander of an operation would issue an order that was addressed specifically to the Minister of the Interior which would detail the role and the duties of the units that were sent by the minister. Other matters that were not of direct interest for the Minister of the Interior would be left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, to your knowledge, what would be the role of these units, police units, or TO units, during such operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: One must distinguish between the police units and the TO units. For instance, the TO units at the strength of a detachment or a battalion could take part in combat activities at the front, forward end, as we put it, whereas police units or units of the Ministry of the Interior secured the implementation of the operation, either by securing roads or buildings or areas. Where companies or units of higher strength were involved, they could also take part in combat activities in the first echelon, but this happened seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said either by securing roads or buildings or areas, what do you exactly mean by "securing areas"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I meant the securing of bridges, saddle passes, or crossroads, or other such features. They could also secure areas from possible ambushes, sabotage actions. They could also provide personal security. And that would be it. There may have been some other tasks that I am not aware of, because I am not that familiar with all the tasks that police units could carry out in terms of providing security.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Babic -- Mr. Maksic, were you present or did you attend any of the meetings or briefings of the 9th Corps of JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember exactly but I attended three or four meetings where normally an analysis would be carried out of the duties performed heretofore, and then they would also deal with prospective tasks. Such meetings were fixed for selected groups of people, depending on what the subject matter was. For instance, we would attend only a part of the meeting dealing with matters that we were in charge of and then we would leave them to discuss other matters. For instance, activities carried out by the 9th Corps at the time constituted a state secret and I did not hold such a position that would enable me to be privy to that. This was true also for all the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During these meetings you were present, were Milan Martic present?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Martic attended two or three meetings, because these meetings had to do with the engagement of some of the units of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now we are talking about some of the units of the Ministry of Interior. To your knowledge, what was -- what was these units? What units were within the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, every town had a police station and certain number of police officers, in charge of protecting and providing security for the citizens and fighting crime in an area. The Ministry of the Interior had an intervention unit as well, I don't know what its strength was, which was ready to be used whenever necessary and wherever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was this intervention unit subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The intervention unit was subordinated to the minister, or to the person designated for that person by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This intervention unit, was it called always in -- I withdraw. Was there other -- I will withdraw my questions. These police units in municipalities, who was their superior?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Every municipality had a commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I show the witness a document, 65 ter 7-8?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you have the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document was issued before you came to Krajina. Can you --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you read what this decision is about?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the setting up of special purpose units of the MUP of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, called the Krajina Police, which are placed within the competence of the Ministry of the Defence." May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I have one specific question. What was this special-purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: These are units for special activities, in charge of fighting sabotage groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what is the difference between a special-purpose unit and an intervention unit, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The difference is almost non-existent. All special purpose units are in fact intervention units for specific periods of time. When there is such need, intervention units or special purpose units can be set up. Normally, their tasks overlap by 80 per cent. Intervention units can be used to prevent rebellion or to restore law and order or to maintain law and order during rallies or demonstrations, whereas special purpose units can perform these tasks as well, although this is not their primary purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what was the primary purpose of this unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: As I've said, their main purpose of special units, you mean, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: They are tasked with fighting infiltrated sabotage groups, arresting and taking into custody enemy sabotage soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which of these units, to your knowledge, participated in the military operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You see, it says on the 29th of 5th -- of May, on the third session, they discussed the setting up of these special-purpose units of MUP, of the SAO Krajina which are to be called the Krajina Police. What follows is actually something that should be called into question. They are placed within the competence of the Ministry of Defence. Now, this may be due to some regulations that they passed in Krajina that I am not aware of but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This is my further question. So please just answer -- always answer my question so we don't overlap our questions and answers. To your knowledge, was this special-purpose unit placed under the authority of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the Article 1 -- I'm sorry, it says also under this decision, that this special-purpose unit to be called the Krajina Police. Is -- was this special-purpose unit called the Krajina Police, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it called like this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. While I was there, it was called the Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The various police units, how they were called?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The Krajina Police was the only name which was used to refer to police units or were there some other names which were used with the police units?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: For as long as I was there, and I speak only about that period, we called it the Krajina Police, pursuant to the constitutional law of Krajina. However, this must not be taken out of the context. This took place on the 29th of May 1991. The only armed forces of Krajina were the Krajina Police. There was no Territorial Defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in -- at the time, when you were already in Krajina, at the end of 1991, were there other -- you mentioned that there were other police units in each municipality. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. Every municipality had its police station, and a number of police officers who took care of the security of the citizens, their private property, fought crime, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that there was always a commander of this police station in respective -- in a respective municipality. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were these commanders subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the Minister of the Interior of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could members of these police station, policemen, participate in any operations by the 9th Corps of JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: In theory, they could. But in practice, in view of their strength, level of training for such activities, they could not really take part in these activities, and I mean these municipal police structures, except for the Krajina Police, this particular unit that we discussed a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So Krajina Police was the unit who could participate in these military operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know how many members had this -- approximately, had this Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You don't know -- I ask approximately. Was it ten, 100, 1.000?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Whatever number I said would be unreliable. This would be my assessment without any basis in what the situation was in reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We were talking about this possibility that -- and you stated it -- that either TO units or Krajina Police units would participate in joint military operations. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also stated that they all were subordinated to the only commander.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The same principle applied both in the army and the police. All the army personnel is subordinated to the Minister of Defence. The same is true for police commanders who are subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When such a police unit is assigned to a task during a joint operation, who would be the superior of this police unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. When --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If there is a joint operation, during which police units participate together with regular army, who would be the superior of this police unit during this operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Whoever is designated by the Minister of the Interior or somebody authorised by the Minister of the Interior. There are two possible options there. If the police unit is resubordinated to the JNA units, then the commander would be the JNA commander. However, if the police simply acts in cooperation or in concert with the JNA units, then the police units would be under the command of the designated commander of the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we have these two variants. If this police unit was subordinated to the commander of the JNA unit, who would be responsible in case they learn that such a policeman committed a crime during this operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Commander of the unit to which the police unit was subordinated. So the commander of the operation is responsible for each individual who participates in that operation, be it a policeman or a soldier. If the unit is resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then you had this second variation, when the police unit only acts in cooperation or in concert with the JNA units, and you say --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Then the commander of that unit would be responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that police units would be under the command of the designated commander of the Ministry of the Interior, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If -- if they are acting in coordination, but if they are acting in the situation where the unit is resubordinated then it's different. Of course, a police unit would have its commander designated by the Minister of the Interior but if the police unit is resubordinated to the JNA unit, then the overall JNA commander would be responsible, and if we have that type of a situation, and if a crime is committed under those circumstances, then the commander of the operation would be responsible, be it police or the military, because he is the one who plans and carries out the operation, and he is the one who is responsible for each individual participating in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, now let's talk about this situation, that it is the JNA commander who is responsible for this overall operation, and he has also this responsibility to punish. What about if this commander fails to punish a member of the police unit who participated in this operation? Does Minister of Interior, as a superior, has any duty if he learns that a police officer committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No, he's not authorised to punish that policeman, at least based on then rules but also based on current rules. What he has to do is to warn the commander of a unit, saying that such and such policeman did this or that, and if no measures are taken, then he needs to inform his own commander in order to ensure that this person will be prosecuted, depending on what kind of an offence it was, whether it was a breach of discipline or a crime, an act which was committed while he was a member of a certain unit, which took part in the operation. Since the Minister of the Interior was not the commander of the operation, nor was the person designated by him, then they cannot be held responsible for a crime committed by a policeman who was resubordinated to a certain commander. A commander is always responsible for acts of his subordinate, regardless of what structure they are coming from, whether it's TO or another structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, I would like to talk a little bit about the relationship between Milan Martic and his Ministry of Interior. And he was a minister, he was a member of government. Milan Babic was president of that government. What was -- to your knowledge, did Milan Babic had any authority over the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the organisation of the government, because Minister of the Interior and all other ministers are all members of the cabinet, of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge, did Milan Martic respond to Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic follow orders receiving from Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The relationship between Milan Martic and Milan Babic was well known, both then and later. Simply speaking, they didn't have a normal type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: While I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean they didn't have a normal type of communication? You said that --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: While I was there, for the duration of three months, I almost never saw them. Actually, not almost; I never saw them together. I never saw them discussing something, agreeing on something and deciding something together. I personally insisted with Babic that they establish some kind of a normal communication because they, the two of them, were the greatest authority figures in Krajina, political authority figures. However, somehow they could never agree on anything. Since I spent more time with Babic, I would frequently try to convince him to do something properly to ensure that their relations become reasonable ones. Once or twice, I'm not sure, I spoke briefly with Mr. Martic, and I gained an impression that it was Milan Babic's fault for the fact that their relations were what I've just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that you spoke briefly with Milan Martic. Can you tell us what did -- what did you discuss with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: We spoke briefly. Once we spoke about the staff. Mr. Martic warned me that I should talk to Babic about it to see what his intentions were, to try to reason with him. I tried to do that. Unfortunately I didn't succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Martic "warned me that I should talk to Babic to see what his intentions were." Can you be more specific when you talk about intentions? What kind of intentions do you have in your mind?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: To put it simply, I can't now quote my words, nor Mr. Martic's words. We wanted them to get together and discuss, define the problems, resolve these problems, and then act in unison at the political scene of Krajina. I tried to convince Babic many times. In this, however, he was quite narcissistic in particular, did not accept anybody else's opinion but his own. Therefore, as I said, unfortunately I did not succeed in this. I now have to qualify my answer. Perhaps there are things I don't know about. Perhaps they met without me knowing about it. I usually knew quite a lot but it is also possible that there were things I didn't know about. It's possible that they met during various cabinet meetings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic -- Mr. Maksic -- it's exactly what the Judges want to hear, only what you know, not what would be your speculation. Can you tell the Judges whether Milan Martic shared any information with the SAO TO?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. I tried two or three times via Mr. Martic's assistant, truth be told it is possible that they did not convey this to him. I tried to get in touch with him and didn't succeed. We received certain reports every night at 8 p.m., and then we would send it to the Ministry of the Interior. Whether that ever reached Mr. Martic or not, I don't know. The reports were supposed to be sent to us by the Ministry of the Interior as well and we never received a single one. I think that they didn't take the TO staff seriously because there were so few of us, just two or three, and they looked at it in a deprecating way. And this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did -- when you are talking about these information, this reports, to your -- and again, only whether you know whether Milan Martic sent these situation reports to Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Milan Martic and his subordinated units, whether they had possibilities to receive information, whether they had established communication system?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had excellent communications. I need to speak -- I need the interpreter to speak up a little bit. I have trouble hearing them. Let me repeat. The question was whether the Ministry of the Interior and its units had good communication channels between them; is that right? Was that your question? Did they have good communication channels; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. My question was, yeah, whether they had well-established communication.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Could you put the volume down a little bit, please? There are two questions in your question. Did they have good communication channels or good communication equipment? What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start with communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Excellent communications equipment, as compared to the ones that the Krajina staff had, as well as the police battalion of the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Because I saw several times their radio stations. They had quite a long range. The sound was clear. I'm not sure I'm finding the right terms right now. So at all times, and in all locations, naturally with some limitations depending on the weather and the geography of the terrain, they were able to establish communications throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, just go back at the beginning of your testimony, when you mentioned this assistance from Ministry of Interior of Republic of Serbia, and you mentioned that they provided some equipment. Do you know where this communication equipment came from?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The units of the interior of Krajina had identical or similar communications equipment as the police of the Republic of Serbia. I suppose that -- not that I suppose; I know that some of the equipment was provided by the Republic of Serbia, in form of an assistance. It was provided to the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina and it was a natural, normal thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Talking about the Ministry of Interior of Republic of Serbia, did you ever see anybody from this ministry coming to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't see a single police official whom I knew, and I knew about a dozen of them. I never saw any of them in Krajina. However, we should distinguish between the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and state security service. These are two different institutions. Several days after my arrival in Knin, I was invited to attend a meeting, Djujic, Kasum, and I were invited. Mr. Martic was present as well, as was Mr. Frenki, whom I didn't know. The name didn't mean anything to me and I simply wasn't interested in the person. However, Kasum and I and Arsa [phoen] who was in charge of the staff communications, were told just before the meeting started, that we were not needed there except for Djujic. On another occasion, Stanisic was present there as well. This didn't mean much to me because I was not familiar with the police and security services. I met Stanisic maybe just once or twice prior to that in a meeting. And then once in Korenica, when there was an incident there, I think that President Bozanic was there. I went there to check something and I met Mr. Martic there and Mr. Frenki. However, I did not attend any meeting, did not take part in any discussions with the associates of Mr. Martic, whose names I don't know. They addressed me as chief. I called them policemen. And we exchanged a few words and then I went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have to clarify here certain points. When you said Mr. Frenki, do you know the whole name of this person?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. Later on I heard his name. It was mentioned in the press and in other places. I can't remember his name right now. It escapes me. Maybe later on I will remember it. I have it written down somewhere in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is this --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: In hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is this name Frenki, is it a second name, first name, or just how this person was called?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. That's a nickname, as far as I understood, it's a nickname. He has a full first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then you mention one Stanisic. Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic. I think that he is from that area, Dalmatia or Lika or somewhere there, but he hails from that area. At the time he was either deputy or chief of the state security service, and they --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you state at the beginning of your statement that "we have to distinguish between Ministry of Interior and state security service because they are different entity," what do you mean that they are a different entity?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: They deal with different things. State security service has one task and police, which is within the Ministry of the Interior, has a different task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is state security service within the Ministry of Interior or outside of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Outside of it, although, after the 5th of October - I don't know if this is important - it became a component of the Ministry of the Interior, but prior to the 5th of October of 2000, state security service was linked to the president of Serbia, whereas the police was under the Ministry of Police. It is true that they have a lot in common, that there is quite a significant overlap in exchange of information, analysis and processing of information. They also sometimes perform joint operations, take joint measures, and it is difficult to draw a line that would separate them strictly. Usually, what is known to the state security service is not known to police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, only if you know, who was superior, who was superior, to this state security service? Did they have any separate ministry? Or who was the superior of this state security service?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Formally and legally speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Maksic, Defence counsel is on his feet. He would like to say something before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. We are now delving into the area of responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior. This witness is not competent either in view of his background or his experience to deal with this. If we are now talking about how this was structured, organised, who was subordinated to whom, this is something beyond the competence of this witness. He can only speak about things that he is familiar with personally. I think that questions should be directed to him bearing this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know that he's not competent, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listened to his biography and based on that I realised that Mr. Maksic was a military person and he only worked for the military. Now he's faced with questions about the Ministry of the Interior, state and public security, and how this was regulated legally. This has to do with a lot of legal issues, and not factual ones, so this is the basis for my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any legal questions that he was asked. I thought he was just being asked about his knowledge of the Ministry of Interior and I think if he doesn't know he will tell us he doesn't know. What he knows, he can answer. Can't he do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any response any way to this objection, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Maksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold on, Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic stated that these two people were from the state security service. It's obvious that he knows about the existence of the state security service. He link it with the Ministry of Interior, so I simply want to know whether he knows who was the superior and exactly, Your Honour, as you stated, he can answer either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The objection is overruled. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to add something to what his -- to what counsel for Defence had to say. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The counsel is quite right, as is his honour. I am not discussing legal matters here. I'm presenting what I saw and what I know. But how these matters are regulated under the law is something I don't know anything about. Therefore, I speak only of things that I saw.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the witness meant "counsel," probably for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then stick to that, Mr. Maksic. Answer what you know, which you saw, which you observed with your own senses. And where you don't know, tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So I would like to repeat my question, whether you know who was the superior of this State Security Service in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: At what point in time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I'm referring to the end of 1991, when you saw Frenki and Jovica Stanisic in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I do have that information but I haven't prepared. I wouldn't know who was head of state security at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness document 65 ter number 207. This document is dated 28th of November 1991, and if we could scroll down to the part we can see the decision? Yes. Thank you. Can we go a little bit up? No, no, no. So we can -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please, can you read what this decision is about?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the relief of duty of the commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. Ilija Djujic, Lieutenant General retired is hereby relieved from the duty of commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina on his own request. This decision shall become effective on the date of its issue. Statement of reason. Ilija Djujic, Lieutenant General, retired" --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to know what this document is about. Does it reflect correctly the situation as it was at the time? Was he relieved from the duty?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: This document has not been compiled properly but this doesn't matter, really, at this stage. It doesn't have a number. But Milan Babic is lying, if I can put it that way, because Ilija Djujic did not ask to be relieved of duty. He wasn't ill. And can you scroll it down, please? Because this statement of reasons here is not true at all. General Djujic was not really active and he agreed with late Tomo Vukovic and I'm not sure whether he went along the same lines as with Milan Martic, about taking over units of the 9th Corps, the weaponry, and the infrastructure. That's to say barracks, gas stations, depots, whatever the 9th Corps had, he espoused this idea of taking hold of all this and we absolutely agreed with him. However, he was able to see the commander of the 9th corps whenever he wanted to. He discussed these matters with him, and they probably agreed on this matter. Babic must have heard about this and removed him, not because of his health condition or age, because even after his removal from duty, he remained active, working in his vineyard and so on. He kept going to -- coming to the staff and he tried to pursue some sort of defence policy of Krajina. This -- Babic's statement of reasons does not reflect the truth. That's what I meant when I said that Babic was lying. And that's all I have to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So the correct thing is that Ilija Djujic was relieved of his duty?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Correct. Because of disagreement as to the concept of Krajina's defence, because of his disagreement with Babic, and not because of his illness. He is not ill today. He is I think in a much better health condition than I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Ilija Djujic stay in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. He hails from there, he has a house and all the outbuildings there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have another document which I would like to show the witness. It's 65 ter number 206. This document is dated 28 of November 1991. If we could scroll down so we can see the decision. Thank you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, could you please read the decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: You mean the text below "decision"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the text below the decision.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: "Prime Minister Milan Babic." Oh, you mean the text above that? "Number 1, Radoslav Maksic, Colonel, is hereby appointed commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. Number 2, this decision shall become effective forthwith." It says -- there is a typo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, did Mr. Babic had authority to appoint you to this position?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: It was solely the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army who had the authority to appoint me to a post. Your Honour, could I have a break just for a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may have a break. Maybe we might as well take an early break and maybe might come back. Court adjourned and we will come back at what time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, that's it. We are adjourned for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
